screens.title: Whiteboxing & Blockouts
screens.narratorSegment: Whiteboxing, also called a blockout, is the fast, low-cost way to sketch a level in 3D before any final assets are made. You use primitive shapes in Unity—cubes, planes, capsules—to test doors, platforms, sightlines, and player movement. The goal is to validate spatial logic and gameplay flow quickly. Imagine building with blocks: it lets you move a whole room or adjust cover without reworking expensive art. This matters because getting scale and navigation right early prevents costly rework later. For example, placing a capsule roughly two units tall as your player lets you check doorway heights, jump distances, and whether cover actually hides a player. A common misconception is to treat the whitebox as a final visual; instead it is a functional sketch. In this lesson you will learn what primitives to use, how to test sightlines and choke points, when to add verticality, and how to move from blockout to art pass. Think of this phase as rapid experiment and conversation between artist and designer: iterate, test, and keep the geometry simple until the gameplay is settled. What would you change first if your player keeps getting stuck?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: In this first set of learning objectives we'll focus on the core skills an artist brings to a whitebox. First, you will understand the purpose and benefits of whiteboxing: why building with primitives saves time, supports rapid iteration, and reduces risk before the art pass. For example, replacing a cube with a building model only after layout is tested avoids expensive asset changes. Second, you will learn to use Unity's primitive 3D objects: Cube, Sphere, Capsule, Cylinder, Plane. Practically, that means placing a Plane for the ground, a Capsule for player scale, and Cubes for walls and cover. Third, you will develop an artistic eye for scale and proportion: you will practice setting door widths, platform heights, and ceiling clearance around a two-unit player reference. Fourth, you will begin to identify gameplay-relevant elements such as cover, choke points, and sightlines using simple geometry and color-coded materials. Each of these skills matters because they let you reason about player experience before polishing visuals. As you practice, ask yourself whether a passage guides the player naturally or feels confusing.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 2
screens.narratorSegment: This second set focuses on practical workflow habits you should adopt during whiteboxing. First, you will practice using color coding and simple materials to mark functional areas—green for cover, red for danger, blue for platforms—so testers instantly understand intent. Second, you will learn to iterate rapidly and test with a player placeholder: move the capsule, try paths, and ask if movement feels natural. Third, you will practice transitioning from blockout to art pass by replacing primitives progressively—begin with low-poly models that match blockout scale before adding textures. Finally, you will learn common pitfalls to avoid: over-detailing the whitebox and ignoring player scale. These habits matter because they turn the blockout from a static sketch into a living design tool used for conversation and testing. For example, a colored cube that marks a cover point communicates tactical intent to teammates during playtests. Keep asking: does this change improve player clarity or just visual fidelity?

screens.title: What is Whiteboxing (Blockout)?
screens.narratorSegment: Whiteboxing is the initial low-fidelity stage where designers and artists use simple geometric primitives to prototype the functional layout of a level. Think of it as a three-dimensional sketch: you are testing spatial relationships, player movement, and gameplay flow rather than visual detail. A concrete example is building a small arena from planes and cubes: a Plane becomes the floor, Cubes become walls and cover, and a Capsule stands in for the player to verify clearances. The whitebox lets you move large elements quickly; swapping a cube's position is far faster than modifying a finished asset. A frequent misconception is that a whitebox must look finished; instead, the whitebox should remain deliberately crude so testing focuses on function. Another contrast is between whiteboxing and mockups: mockups often focus on visual fidelity while whiteboxes prioritize player experience. Key checks include whether doorways fit a two-unit player, if sightlines permit predictable combat, and whether choke points create intended tension. The takeaway is simple: keep geometry minimal, test early and often, and treat the whitebox as a communication tool between art and design. keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A whitebox is a rapid, low-fidelity 3D sketch used to test spatial layout and gameplay before final art is applied.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is Whiteboxing?
A working, low-fidelity 3D sketch that prioritizes function over form.
Why it matters
  • Lets teams validate scale and flow without final art.
  • Enables rapid movement of large geometry during iteration.
  • Reduces costly rework later in development.
Example
Build a 10x10 plane floor, place cubes as walls and cover, add a 2-unit capsule to check doorway heights and jump reaches.
Key Takeaway

Keep geometry simple. Test scale and sightlines first; replace art later.

Blockout Anatomy
Primitives
Cube, Plane, Capsule, Cylinder used as placeholders for buildings, floors, players and obstacles.
Player Reference
A capsule set to roughly 2 units tall to test doors, platform reach, and movement collisions.
Functional Areas
Color-code zones for cover, hazard, and traversal during playtests.
Iteration
Move large elements quickly and run early playtests; adjust scale and flow before adding art.

screens.title: Using Unity Primitives Effectively
screens.narratorSegment: Working with Unity primitives is straightforward, but doing it with intent makes your blockout effective. Start by creating a Plane for the ground sized to your design (for example, 10 by 10 units for a small arena). Next, add a Capsule at roughly (0, 1, 0) to act as the player placeholder — this 2-unit tall reference anchors all other decisions. Third, use Cubes for walls, platforms and basic cover. Scale cubes in X, Y, and Z to form doorways, barricades, and short vs tall cover. Fourth, add Cylinders for columns or rounded obstacles that change sightlines. At each step, test navigation by moving the capsule along intended paths. A concrete run: place two large Cubes to make a corridor, then instantiate smaller Cubes as waist-high cover; try crouching or moving through the corridor to check if cover actually blocks sight. A common mistake is forgetting to align primitives to the floor or leaving gaps that trap a player. The key idea is to iterate rapidly: tweak a cube's size, retest, and repeat until pathways, cover, and sightlines feel intentional. After this process, you'll have a functional layout ready for playtesting and eventual art replacement. Which step would you iterate first after a playtest?

keyIdea.title: Workflow steps
keyIdea.text: Plane → Capsule → Cubes/Cylinders → test navigation → iterate until paths and cover work.

content.html:
Process Flow
Using Unity Primitives
A quick step sequence to build a functional blockout.
Step 1 — Ground Plane
Add a Plane and scale to arena size, e.g., 10x10 units for a small arena.
Step 2 — Player Capsule
Place a Capsule at player start, about 2 units tall, to check clearances.
Step 3 — Walls & Cover
Use Cubes for walls and different sized cover; vary heights to create tactical choices.
Step 4 — Rounded Obstacles
Cylinders are useful for columns and for breaking straight sightlines.
Key Takeaway

Build iteratively: place primitive, test with player placeholder, adjust scale and position until gameplay feels right.

Guided Example
Arena Blockout Example
Ground: Plane scaled to X=10 Z=10. Player: Capsule at Y=1. Walls: Cubes 10x3x0.5. Cover: smaller cubes and cylinders at varying heights. Test: move the capsule through the arena, check that short cover blocks line of sight when crouched or standing.
Common Mistake
Misaligned primitives that leave collision gaps or unreachable ledges; always snap to the floor and test movement.
Pro Tip
Use simple unlit materials with bright colors to communicate function quickly during playtests.

screens.title: Player Scale & Proportion
screens.narratorSegment: Player scale is the most important reference in a blockout because it directly affects movement, visibility, and comfort. In Unity workflows, a standard capsule around two units tall is a reliable starting point. When you test doorways, stairs, and platform gaps against this capsule you immediately see whether movement feels natural. For example, a doorway that is only 1.2 units wide will cause cramped navigation for a two-unit player; increasing width to 2.5 units or more often improves flow. A common misunderstanding is to size things by eye rather than by a physical reference; this leads to inconsistent clearances across the level. Compare two scenarios: in the first, platforms are placed without a capsule and players struggle to reach edges; in the second, platforms are positioned with capsule testing and jumps feel fair and repeatable. Use direct testing: move the capsule through doorways, try jumping to platforms, and check for moments where the capsule clips geometry. Always keep a simple checklist: door height, doorway width, platform reachability, ceiling clearance, and step-up heights. This keeps your blockout grounded in player experience rather than visual guesswork. Which of those checks is most likely to catch a problem early in your designs?

keyIdea.title: Scale rule
keyIdea.text: Use a 2-unit player capsule as the constant reference to ensure consistent navigation and comfortable proportions.

content.html:
Comparison
Player Scale & Proportion
Practical checks that prevent navigation problems.
Scenario A — No Player Reference
Design by eye; leads to inconsistent doorways and unreachable platforms that only appear during playtests.
Scenario B — With 2-unit Capsule
Use the capsule to size doors, platforms, and ceilings; movement tests catch problems early.
Key Takeaway

Make the player capsule your ruler. It prevents inconsistent scaling and saves time in iteration.

Quick Checklist
  • Door height and width meet capsule clearance.
  • Platform jump distances are reachable from capsule start height.
  • Ceiling clearance prevents clipping at head height.
  • Step-up heights are comfortable to traverse without unintended climbs.
Example
Adjust a doorway from 1.2 to 2.6 units wide after capsule testing to reduce jamming points.
Common Mistake
Designers gauging scale visually without a player reference end up with inconsistent gameplay zones.
Reflect: which clearance measurement will you standardize across your level?

screens.title: Sightlines, Cover, and Choke Points
screens.narratorSegment: Sightlines, cover, and choke points are fundamental gameplay elements you can develop and test in a whitebox quickly. Sightlines describe what a player can see from a position; they affect combat balance and exploration. Using cubes and cylinders, you can create long corridors for long-range engagements or staggered cover that encourages movement. Cover objects should be sized and placed so they provide meaningful protection when the player uses them; for instance, a waist-high cube blocks line of sight when crouched but allows over-the-top fire when standing. Choke points are narrow connections that funnel players and create tension; blockouts let you adjust their width and approach angles to tune difficulty. A practical technique is color-coding: mark green objects as cover, red zones as exposed, and blue for traversal. During a playtest, a quick visual read of those colors reveals whether your intended tactical flow actually emerges. A common misconception is that more cover always improves gameplay; in practice, too many cover objects can stall movement and reduce decision-making. The key takeaway: craft sightlines and cover intentionally in the blockout, then test repeatedly with players to confirm your design assumptions. Where might a sightline reveal an unintended advantage for a player?

keyIdea.title: Tactical tools
keyIdea.text: Use primitives to prototype sightlines, cover, and choke points; color-code functions to speed testing and communication.

content.html:
Design Focus
Sightlines, Cover & Choke Points
Tune tactical play by arranging simple geometry and color codes.
Sightlines
Test visibility from key vantage points to ensure balanced encounters and meaningful exploration.
Cover
Size cover so it functions as intended: short for crouch, tall for full protection.
Choke Points
Narrow funnels create tension but can block flow if overused; balance with open areas.
Example Scenario
Arena Entrance Test
Create a narrow doorway using two Cubes and place staggered cover in the room. Color the doorway red to mark danger and cover in green. Have a tester approach from multiple angles to see if cover actually creates tactical choices.
Common Mistake
Placing too many identical cover objects that make encounters repetitive and slow down movement.
Pro Tip
Use cylinders or angled cubes to break predictable sightlines and encourage movement around cover.
Challenge: can you reduce a choke point without losing its tactical function?

screens.title: Verticality & Elevation
screens.narratorSegment: Verticality adds a third dimension to your level that can create strategic depth and movement variety. In a whitebox, use stacked Cubes and platforms to prototype stairs, ledges, and elevated positions. Always test these elements with the player capsule to make sure jumps and step-ups are reachable. A simple example is placing a cube platform one unit higher than the ground to see if the capsule can step up without clipping; another is creating a two-unit headroom under an overhang to ensure the player can stand comfortably. Verticality changes sightlines: raised positions give advantage or new perspectives, while pits or low areas can create danger zones. Misconceptions include adding vertical complexity without clear navigation; avoid levels that force the player to guess how to reach higher platforms. Use hierarchy in your blockout: mark primary vertical routes (stairs or ramps), secondary platforms (optional vantage points), and forbidden drops. Color-code these levels—blue for primary traversal, green for optional—so playtesters immediately understand navigational intent. The takeaway: prototype vertical elements early, test with a capsule, and ensure each vertical choice adds meaningful decisions instead of confusion. What vertical path would you add to create a rewarding flank?

content.html:
Hierarchy
Verticality & Elevation
Design vertical layers that support movement and tactical choices.
Primary Routes
Stairs and ramps that players use to move reliably between levels.
Secondary Platforms
Optional vantage points or flanking ledges that reward exploration.
Forbidden Drops
Clear visual cues for dangerous falls or inaccessible areas to avoid player confusion.
Key Takeaway

Prototype vertical elements early and test reachability with the player capsule to keep movement intuitive.

Example Layout
Two-level Arena
Create a raised platform reachable by a 1-unit ramp. Place waist-high cover on the platform to test whether the elevated position provides meaningful control over the ground area.
Common Mistake
Adding elevated areas without clear paths makes players feel lost; always provide logical traversal routes.
Playtest Prompt
Ask testers: can you reach this platform naturally? Is the elevated view worth the effort?

screens.title: From Blockout to Art Pass
screens.narratorSegment: The art pass is the stage where whitebox geometry is gradually replaced with actual models, textures, and props. The best practice is to replace objects progressively, not all at once. Start by swapping a Cube that represented a building with a low-polygon version of the intended model that matches the blockout's scale and position. Confirm collisions and sightlines after each replacement. Then iterate by adding textures and detail in stages: coarse geometry, low-poly art, then textures and props. A useful technique is to parent new art to the blockout object initially so positional relationships remain exact. Another practical point is to keep color-coded materials for functionality until you are confident the new assets preserve gameplay intent. A common pitfall is replacing art before playtesting the blockout sufficiently — this can lock in mistakes. Also avoid assuming final art will be identical to primitives; modelers will adapt shape but should preserve the spatial footprint. The takeaway: use the blockout as a scaffold and test after each swap to ensure scale, cover, and sightlines are preserved. How will you verify a replaced cover still provides the same tactical protection?

narration.text: The art pass is the stage where whitebox geometry is gradually replaced with actual models, textures, and props. The best practice is to replace objects progressively, not all at once. screens.title: Playtesting & Iteration
screens.narratorSegment: Iteration and playtesting are the heartbeat of a successful whitebox process. Run short, focused tests: watch a player move from point A to B, observe where they hesitate, and note any stuck spots. Use the capsule to try corner cases yourself—can it clip into a wall? Does jumping produce predictable results? When you gather feedback, prioritize changes that affect navigation and clarity: widen confusing doorways, reduce repetitive cover, or create clearer routes to objectives. A common mistake is treating playtests as a one-time check; instead, make iteration a loop. After each change, run another short test rather than waiting for a final session. You can also use simple color cues to test intent: if testers misinterpret a green cover block as an obstacle, you have a communication issue to fix, not an art problem. Keep changes intentionally large early on—small tweaks that don't change the player's understanding often waste time. The takeaway: iterate quickly, test early, and focus on player experience metrics like movement fluidity, sightline clarity, and encounter fairness. Process
Playtesting & Iteration
How to run focused tests and translate feedback into blockout changes.
Short Test Routine
1. Watch a tester move between two points. 2. Note hesitation and stuck spots. 3. Make a single geometry change. 4. Retest immediately.
Prioritize Changes
Fix navigation and clarity first. Cosmetic tweaks come later during the art pass.
Communication
Use colored materials and labels to make test intent obvious and reduce misinterpretation during feedback sessions.
Key Takeaway

Treat playtesting as an iterative loop: test, change, and retest until the level communicates movement and choices clearly.

Example Feedback Cycle
Observed Issue
Testers consistently hug the left wall and miss the intended door. Fix: widen entry and add a small visual cue at the doorway, then retest.
Common Mistake
Making too many small changes after a test, which blurs cause and effect. Change one thing at a time.
Pro Tip
Record short clips of tester runs to see subtle navigation issues you might miss live.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Several common mistakes recur in whiteboxing; knowing them helps you stay efficient. First, over-detailing the whitebox wastes time: adding high-polygon models or complex materials before layout is confirmed shifts focus away from gameplay. Keep details minimal until the design is locked. Second, neglecting player scale is a recipe for navigation problems—always test with a capsule or player placeholder and verify doorways, ceilings, and jump distances. Third, failing to iterate and playtest early often leads to late-stage redesigns; run short tests as soon as you can and adjust major elements first. Fourth, misusing cover by repeating identical objects creates stale encounters; vary cover sizes and positions to force decisions. Finally, assuming final art will match primitives exactly can introduce surprises; instead, use progressive swaps and re-verify behavior. A useful checklist before moving to the art pass: player-scale verification, sightline checks from key vantage points, cover functionality tests, and a short playtest loop with at least one external tester. The takeaway is to keep the blockout purposeful, test-driven, and intentionally crude until gameplay is confirmed. Which of these mistakes are you most likely to catch quickly in your next blockout?

Whiteboxing, also called a blockout, is the fast, low-cost way to sketch a level in 3D before any final assets are made. You use primitive shapes in Unity—cubes, planes, capsules—to test doors, platforms, sightlines, and player movement. The goal is to validate spatial logic and gameplay flow quickly. Imagine building with blocks: it lets you move a whole room or adjust cover without reworking expensive art. This matters because getting scale and navigation right early prevents costly rework later. For example, placing a capsule roughly two units tall as your player lets you check doorway heights, jump distances, and whether cover actually hides a player. A common misconception is to treat the whitebox as a final visual; instead it is a functional sketch. In this lesson you will learn what primitives to use, how to test sightlines and choke points, when to add verticality, and how to move from blockout to art pass. Think of this phase as rapid experiment and conversation between artist and designer: iterate, test, and keep the geometry simple until the gameplay is settled. What would you change first if your player keeps getting stuck?

In this first set of learning objectives we'll focus on the core skills an artist brings to a whitebox. First, you will understand the purpose and benefits of whiteboxing: why building with primitives saves time, supports rapid iteration, and reduces risk before the art pass. For example, replacing a cube with a building model only after layout is tested avoids expensive asset changes. Second, you will learn to use Unity's primitive 3D objects: Cube, Sphere, Capsule, Cylinder, Plane. Practically, that means placing a Plane for the ground, a Capsule for player scale, and Cubes for walls and cover. Third, you will develop an artistic eye for scale and proportion: you will practice setting door widths, platform heights, and ceiling clearance around a two-unit player reference. Fourth, you will begin to identify gameplay-relevant elements such as cover, choke points, and sightlines using simple geometry and color-coded materials. Each of these skills matters because they let you reason about player experience before polishing visuals. As you practice, ask yourself whether a passage guides the player naturally or feels confusing.

This second set focuses on practical workflow habits you should adopt during whiteboxing. First, you will practice using color coding and simple materials to mark functional areas—green for cover, red for danger, blue for platforms—so testers instantly understand intent. Second, you will learn to iterate rapidly and test with a player placeholder: move the capsule, try paths, and ask if movement feels natural. Third, you will practice transitioning from blockout to art pass by replacing primitives progressively—begin with low-poly models that match blockout scale before adding textures. Finally, you will learn common pitfalls to avoid: over-detailing the whitebox and ignoring player scale. These habits matter because they turn the blockout from a static sketch into a living design tool used for conversation and testing. For example, a colored cube that marks a cover point communicates tactical intent to teammates during playtests. Keep asking: does this change improve player clarity or just visual fidelity?

Whiteboxing is the initial low-fidelity stage where designers and artists use simple geometric primitives to prototype the functional layout of a level. Think of it as a three-dimensional sketch: you are testing spatial relationships, player movement, and gameplay flow rather than visual detail. A concrete example is building a small arena from planes and cubes: a Plane becomes the floor, Cubes become walls and cover, and a Capsule stands in for the player to verify clearances. The whitebox lets you move large elements quickly; swapping a cube's position is far faster than modifying a finished asset. A frequent misconception is that a whitebox must look finished; instead, the whitebox should remain deliberately crude so testing focuses on function. Another contrast is between whiteboxing and mockups: mockups often focus on visual fidelity while whiteboxes prioritize player experience. Key checks include whether doorways fit a two-unit player, if sightlines permit predictable combat, and whether choke points create intended tension. The takeaway is simple: keep geometry minimal, test early and often, and treat the whitebox as a communication tool between art and design. Which path feels most natural to a player in your current blockout?

Working with Unity primitives is straightforward, but doing it with intent makes your blockout effective. Start by creating a Plane for the ground sized to your design (for example, 10 by 10 units for a small arena). Next, add a Capsule at roughly (0, 1, 0) to act as the player placeholder — this 2-unit tall reference anchors all other decisions. Third, use Cubes for walls, platforms and basic cover. Scale cubes in X, Y, and Z to form doorways, barricades, and short vs tall cover. Fourth, add Cylinders for columns or rounded obstacles that change sightlines. At each step, test navigation by moving the capsule along intended paths. A concrete run: place two large Cubes to make a corridor, then instantiate smaller Cubes as waist-high cover; try crouching or moving through the corridor to check if cover actually blocks sight. A common mistake is forgetting to align primitives to the floor or leaving gaps that trap a player. The key idea is to iterate rapidly: tweak a cube's size, retest, and repeat until pathways, cover, and sightlines feel intentional. After this process, you'll have a functional layout ready for playtesting and eventual art replacement. Which step would you iterate first after a playtest?

Player scale is the most important reference in a blockout because it directly affects movement, visibility, and comfort. In Unity workflows, a standard capsule around two units tall is a reliable starting point. When you test doorways, stairs, and platform gaps against this capsule you immediately see whether movement feels natural. For example, a doorway that is only 1.2 units wide will cause cramped navigation for a two-unit player; increasing width to 2.5 units or more often improves flow. A common misunderstanding is to size things by eye rather than by a physical reference; this leads to inconsistent clearances across the level. Compare two scenarios: in the first, platforms are placed without a capsule and players struggle to reach edges; in the second, platforms are positioned with capsule testing and jumps feel fair and repeatable. Use direct testing: move the capsule through doorways, try jumping to platforms, and check for moments where the capsule clips geometry. Always keep a simple checklist: door height, doorway width, platform reachability, ceiling clearance, and step-up heights. This keeps your blockout grounded in player experience rather than visual guesswork. Which of those checks is most likely to catch a problem early in your designs?

Sightlines, cover, and choke points are fundamental gameplay elements you can develop and test in a whitebox quickly. Sightlines describe what a player can see from a position; they affect combat balance and exploration. Using cubes and cylinders, you can create long corridors for long-range engagements or staggered cover that encourages movement. Cover objects should be sized and placed so they provide meaningful protection when the player uses them; for instance, a waist-high cube blocks line of sight when crouched but allows over-the-top fire when standing. Choke points are narrow connections that funnel players and create tension; blockouts let you adjust their width and approach angles to tune difficulty. A practical technique is color-coding: mark green objects as cover, red zones as exposed, and blue for traversal. During a playtest, a quick visual read of those colors reveals whether your intended tactical flow actually emerges. A common misconception is that more cover always improves gameplay; in practice, too many cover objects can stall movement and reduce decision-making. The key takeaway: craft sightlines and cover intentionally in the blockout, then test repeatedly with players to confirm your design assumptions. Where might a sightline reveal an unintended advantage for a player?

Verticality adds a third dimension to your level that can create strategic depth and movement variety. In a whitebox, use stacked Cubes and platforms to prototype stairs, ledges, and elevated positions. Always test these elements with the player capsule to make sure jumps and step-ups are reachable. A simple example is placing a cube platform one unit higher than the ground to see if the capsule can step up without clipping; another is creating a two-unit headroom under an overhang to ensure the player can stand comfortably. Verticality changes sightlines: raised positions give advantage or new perspectives, while pits or low areas can create danger zones. Misconceptions include adding vertical complexity without clear navigation; avoid levels that force the player to guess how to reach higher platforms. Use hierarchy in your blockout: mark primary vertical routes (stairs or ramps), secondary platforms (optional vantage points), and forbidden drops. Color-code these levels—blue for primary traversal, green for optional—so playtesters immediately understand navigational intent. The takeaway: prototype vertical elements early, test with a capsule, and ensure each vertical choice adds meaningful decisions instead of confusion.
